newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland's Kone says profits plunge.
newsitem.headline: Finland's Kone says profits plunge.

text.p: Kone Oy, a world-leading Finnish elevator and escalator group, on Thursday reported a 79 percent slump in profits and repeated a dim view on its prospects.
Reporting January-August earnings after financial items down to 14 million markka ($3.06 million) from 66 million in the year-ago period, Kone repeated a forecast of near-zero net earnings for 1996.

"Kone's after-tax income for 1996 will not reach the previous year's level and is expected to be about zero. The result for 1997 will only be slightly better," Kone said in a statement with its January-August results.
For full year 1995, Kone reported net income of 67 million markka and profit after financial items of 202 million markka.
The company warned on September 19 it expected near-zero earnings for 1996 due to problems in its Italian operations where losses would approach 200 million markka for 1996.

"Correcting these problems is proving more costly and time-consuming than was originally anticipated," Kone said on Thursday. "Measures currently being implemented are expected to return Kone's Italian operations to profitability during 1997."
Kone said it may book slightly higher orders in 1996 than in 1995 but prices would remain poor.
"Price competition continues to be extremely tough in all geographical areas and business sectors," Kone said.

Its report included from July 1 the results of German escalator maker O&K Rolltreppen acquired in summer, but the company said much of the German company's sales were already handled by various Kone companies so its impact was slight.
Kone said it expected full-year 1996 sales to reach about 10 billion markka at current exchange rates, up from 9.52 billion in 1995.

Its total sales in January-August rose by some seven percent to 6.01 billion markka. Kone said new elevator and escalator sales accounted for about 34 percent of total turnover with maintenance and modernisation making up the remainder.

Kone said the value of new orders excluding maintenance sales rose by about 10 percent to 4.87 billion. It said this increase would only have been about four percent without new acquisitions and the impact of currency fluctuations.
"Orders received for the whole of 1996 will probably exceed slightly those for the previous year, but the price level will remain poor," Kone said.
Demand for its new space-saving elevator concept had got off to a promising start: "Its impact on Kone's result, however, will only become tangible in future years."
